name: Calcium hydroxylapatite filler (Radiesse)

lead: Calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA) filler, best known by the brand name Radiesse, is a gel containing tiny calcium-based microspheres. Clinicians inject it to add volume and structure to areas such as the cheeks, jawline and chin, and it is also described as stimulating the body's own collagen.

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a firmer, 'high G prime' option for a more defined jaw or chin without surgery. Published research mostly concerns older patients rather than young people seeking facial definition.

paras: The gel carrier gives immediate volume while the microspheres act as a scaffold. Reviews describe nearby cells responding by producing collagen, elastin and other tissue components, with the gel itself gradually absorbed.

A review of 21 studies covering 5,081 treatments reported adverse events in about 3 percent of treatments, almost all nodules [4]. Fillers as a category carry a rare but serious risk of vascular occlusion, including blindness [12]. In the US, fillers are regulated as medical devices that a provider must inject [19]; approved indications for Radiesse are limited, and many facial contouring uses are off-label [2].

lead: Calcium hydroxylapatite filler, sold most prominently as Radiesse (Merz Aesthetics), is an injectable soft-tissue filler made of calcium hydroxylapatite microspheres suspended in a carboxymethylcellulose gel [1][2]. It is classed as a biostimulatory filler because, besides giving immediate volume, it is reported to induce new collagen, elastin and blood vessel formation in the surrounding tissue [1].

Clinicians use it for wrinkles and folds, cheek and jawline contouring, facial lipoatrophy in people with HIV and hand rejuvenation; off-label uses include skin tightening with diluted or hyperdiluted preparations [2][3]. In looksmaxxing communities it appears under the label 'high G prime filler', as a firmer non-surgical option for adding structure to the jaw, chin and cheekbones.

A 2024 systematic review concluded that CaHA/CMC may be considered a safe and effective option for the cheeks, jawline, HIV-related lipoatrophy and nasolabial folds, while noting that no randomized controlled trials had been published on diluted and hyperdiluted techniques [2]. A review of the safety literature found nodules to be by far the most commonly reported adverse event [4].

paras: Radiesse consists of calcium hydroxylapatite microspheres suspended in a carboxymethylcellulose gel. The gel gives an immediate effect and is gradually absorbed, while the microspheres act as a scaffold for cells [1]. Reviewers link its robust rheological properties, meaning how it resists deformation under force, to its versatility for volumizing and contouring [2].

A laboratory study compared the viscosity and elasticity of CaHA and cross-linked hyaluronic acid (HA) fillers, aiming to give physicians a scientific rationale for choosing a product for volume replacement [5]. This difference in stiffness underlies the community term 'high G prime', where G prime refers to a gel's elastic firmness.

Reviewers describe on-label uses of CaHA/CMC as filling wrinkles and lines, volumizing and contouring, and off-label uses as biostimulation and skin tightening [2]. On the body, the only FDA-approved indication reported in a 2024 review is the hands, with a European Union approval for the decolletage [3].

A systematic review reported that CaHA/CMC appears safe and effective for the cheeks and jawline, and that marionette lines, chin, pre-jowl area and mouth corners also tend to respond with a high degree of efficacy [2]. A review of lower-face reshaping describes the jawline as central to a youthful, sexually dimorphic appearance and discusses fillers as a way to redefine the mandibular angle and line [6].

Evidence is mostly drawn from ageing or volume-depleted patients. No published trial identified here was designed around young adults seeking skeletal-looking definition, which is the goal most often described in looksmaxxing forums.
CaHA/CMC has been used for HIV-related facial lipoatrophy [2] and for hand volume loss [7]. ClinicalTrials.gov also lists studies of CaHA for cellulite dimples in the buttocks [8].

Facial evidence consists largely of observational studies, case series and histology comparisons, which systematic reviewers summarise as showing efficacy for the cheeks, jawline and nasolabial folds [2]. For body treatment and for diluted or hyperdiluted products, reviewers state that current trends and guidelines have yet to be supported by randomized controlled trials, despite a good safety profile in clinical practice [3][2].

A multicenter randomized trial examined the long-term duration and safety of Radiesse (+) for the jawline [9]. A randomized split-face study in 24 women aged 35 to 45 compared biopsies after Radiesse with those after a hyaluronic acid filler to examine collagen and elastin production [10]. A randomized comparison of gene expression after poly-L-lactic acid and CaHA injection reported that the two biostimulators act through different pathways, and its title describes CaHA as inducing inflammation [11]. A pilot study of diluted CaHA in the neck and decolletage examined neocollagenesis and skin mechanical properties [12].

A review of 21 articles covering 5,081 treatments in 2,779 patients found 173 adverse events (3 percent), of which 96 percent were nodules; the rest were persistent swelling, persistent redness and overcorrection. About half the nodules occurred in dynamic areas, and in most cases nodules were not visible and resolved without intervention [4].

As with other fillers, injection into or compression of blood vessels can cause tissue damage or vision loss. A review of cases of blindness after cosmetic filler injection describes the complication as rare but greatly feared, and reported cases as mostly irreversible [13]. Wikipedia's overview lists bruising, redness and pain as the common effects of dermal fillers [14].

Human studies include systematic reviews of facial and body use [2][3], a safety review of 21 articles [4], randomized trials comparing CaHA with hyaluronic acid or poly-L-lactic acid or assessing the jawline [10][11][9], and a prospective trial of chest rejuvenation [15]. Reviewers note that no randomized controlled trials have been published on diluted or hyperdiluted use [2].

Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include a study of cheek flattening [16], a Phase 4 trial of restoring facial volume after GLP-1 weight loss [17] and a study of Radiesse for nasolabial folds [18].

On looksmax.org, discussion of hydroxyapatite more often concerns solid facial implants than the injectable. One thread starter describes hydroxyapatite implants as the closest material to bone and says they should be discussed more, while a reply argues that implant material barely matters [19].

lore.intro: Community discussion places CaHA among 'structure' fillers used for jaw and chin definition, and it is sometimes discussed alongside hydroxyapatite bone implants [19].

claims.claim: High G prime filler can mimic bone and sharpen the jaw or chin without surgery.
Hydroxyapatite is the closest material to real bone and the best facial implant material.
